description: Domain-specific question pools for Phase 1 prototype. Layer 2 of the offline selector. Three pool types: occasion (birthday/wedding/graduation/after-my-death/whenever-you-need-this), relationship (child/partner/friend/sibling), and heavy-gated domains (apology/regret/fear/spiritual/permission/grief). Heavy pools require at least one prior lower-intensity pass this session or explicit author opt-in.
notes: All intensity-3 questions are gated. Never surface them as session openers.
No question may assume faith, parenthood, happy family structure, or resolved conflict.
Do not mutate at runtime. User-local state lives in ~/.lateletter/author/ only.
review_status: draft — not editorially reviewed, prototype only.

birthday.description: For messages tied to a specific birthday. Focus: who this person is at this age, what you see in them, memories of who they've been, hopes for where they're going.

questions.prompt: What do you see in them now that you didn't know to look for when they were younger?
What do you hope they feel about themselves at this age?
What's something about who they've become that fills you with pride — not an achievement, just who they are?
What do you remember about them at a much earlier age that still feels vivid to you?
What do you want them to believe about their own future?
Is there something they were once unsure of about themselves that has resolved — something they got right?
What advice would you give them for the decade ahead?
What would you want to celebrate about them if you could be there?
What has watching them grow — or watching them become who they are — meant to you?
If they're reading this on a birthday without you, what do you most want them to feel?
follow_up_hints: Good closer for birthday messages.

wedding.description: For messages tied to a wedding or commitment ceremony. Focus: what partnership and love mean to you, what you see in this relationship, hopes for their shared life.

questions.prompt: What do you hope for their partnership — not the romance, but the daily texture of a shared life?
What do you know about love that took you years to understand?
What do you see in them that makes you believe they're ready for this?
What do you most want them to remember when things are hard between them?
Is there something you'd want to tell them about choosing a person over and over — not once, but every day?
What have you learned about forgiveness in long relationships?
What do you hope they protect in each other?
What do you think makes a lasting partnership?
If you could give them one piece of advice that took you a long time to earn, what would it be?

graduation.description: For messages tied to a graduation or major transition. Focus: becoming, what's ahead, advice from a different vantage point, what you see in them as they step into what's next.

questions.prompt: What do you see ahead for them that they might not see yet?
What do you hope they know about themselves as they step into what's next?
What do you wish someone had told you at this moment in your own life?
What do you want them to remember about how hard they worked to get here?
What do you hope they hold onto, even as everything changes?
Is there something about the world they're entering that you want them to be prepared for?
What do you believe about failure that you'd want them to carry into this next chapter?
What does success mean to you, and how do you hope they define it for themselves?

after_my_death.description: For messages explicitly intended to arrive after the author has died. The heaviest occasion type. Focus: farewell, permission-giving, what to carry forward, how to grieve. Mix of intensity 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: What do you most want them to know about how you feel about your life?
follow_up_hints: Good opener for this occasion type.

questions.prompt: Is there anything you want to say about how you hope they grieve — or when they stop?
What do you want them to carry forward from knowing you?
What do you want them to know about what the time you had with them meant?
What would you want them to tell people they love about you — not a eulogy, just something true?
If they feel your absence most on ordinary days, what do you want them to know then?
Is there anything you'd want them to do — or give themselves permission to do — after you're gone?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Only after at least one lower-intensity exchange in this session.

questions.prompt: What do you hope they don't spend too long on — grief, guilt, or feeling they should have done something differently?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Permission-releasing framing — author absolves, not burdens.

questions.prompt: What do you want them to know about who they are — what they are capable of — without you?
follow_up_hints: Gated. One of the most important things a letter like this can say.

whenever_you_need_this.description: For messages with no fixed date — delivered whenever the recipient opens it or triggers it. Focus: comfort, presence, reassurance in hard moments.

questions.prompt: If they're struggling right now, what do you want them to hear from you?
What do you want them to remember about their own strength?
What do you most want them to know when things feel too hard?
What do you hope they allow themselves when they're hurting — rest, anger, asking for help?
What do you know about hard times that you'd want them to hold onto?
If they're doubting themselves right now, what truth about them would you want them to come back to?
Is there something from their past — something they've already survived — that you'd want them to draw on?

child.description: For messages to the author's child (any age). Focus: parenthood, what watching them grow has meant, what you see in them, hopes for their life. Does not assume a happy family structure — all prompts work for complicated relationships too.

questions.prompt: What was it like to first know them — to see who they were going to be?
What do you hope you gave them — not things, but something they carry?
What do you most want them to understand about how much they are loved?
What do you see in them now that you'd want them to see in themselves?
Is there something parenthood surprised you with — something you didn't expect to learn?
What do you hope they know about the kind of person they are?
What do you hope they carry forward from your family — the good parts?
What do you want them to know about mistakes — yours, theirs — and whether they define a person?
What do you hope for them as a parent someday, if that becomes part of their life?
follow_up_hints: Only use if author has indicated child wants children or hasn't said either way.

questions.prompt: Is there anything about your own childhood — something that shaped you — you'd want them to understand?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Can surface unresolved family history. Only after lower-intensity pass.

partner.description: For messages to a spouse, partner, or long-term intimate partner. Focus: intimacy, the private texture of a shared life, what being loved by them has meant, what you hope for their future. Does not assume a happy marriage.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to you to have been loved by them?
What have they taught you about yourself?
What do you most want them to know about what your time together has meant?
What do you love about how they move through the world — the way they are with people, with life?
What do you want them to remember about the two of you at your best?
Is there something you've always wanted to say about how they've changed you?
Is there a way they've made you better that they might not even know about?
What do you want them to know about what they've given you — not done for you, but given you?
What do you hope they allow themselves after you — happiness, connection, a life that is fully theirs?
follow_up_hints: Gated. The most important permission a partner can give. Only after lower-intensity pass.

friend.description: For messages to a close friend. Focus: chosen connection, what their friendship has meant, what you'd want them to carry forward. Works for lifelong friends and newer but important ones.

questions.prompt: What has this friendship meant to you?
What do you appreciate most about who they are as a person — not what they do, just who they are?
What do you want them to know about how they've shown up for you?
Is there something about your friendship that you've always hoped they understood?
What do you hope they know about the kind of friend they are?
What would you want them to remember about your time together?
What do you most want them to carry forward from knowing you?
What do you wish you'd said more often?
follow_up_hints: Good closer for friend letters. Opens space for anything unsaid.

sibling.description: For messages to a sibling. Focus: shared history, what siblinghood has meant, the family you came from, what you hope they carry. Does not assume a close or uncomplicated relationship.

questions.prompt: What do you remember about growing up together that you want them to know still matters to you?
What have they always understood about you that others haven't?
What do you most appreciate about who they are — as a sibling, as a person?
What do you hope they know about how you've felt about them, even when it was hard to say?
What would you want to tell them about family — what it's meant to you, what you hope it means to them?
What do you want them to carry forward from your time as siblings?
Is there something from your shared history — something between the two of you — you'd want to name out loud in this letter?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Can surface unresolved family dynamics. Use only after lower-intensity pass.

apology.description: Gated pool for authors who want to acknowledge harm or ask forgiveness. All questions intensity 3. Only surfaced after explicit author opt-in or after at least one lower-intensity pass. No question implies the author must apologize — framing is permissive, not directive.

questions.prompt: Is there something you've done or said — or failed to do — that you'd want to acknowledge in this letter?
follow_up_hints: Permissive framing — author may say no. Do not follow with pressure.

questions.prompt: Is there something between you that you've hoped, over the years, they could forgive?
Is there a moment you'd go back and handle differently, and do you want to say so to them?
What do you want them to know about how you see your own failures — not to excuse them, but to own them?
If this letter holds space for an apology, what would you most want to say?
follow_up_hints: Most direct apology prompt. Use after author has already opened up in this domain.

regret.description: Gated pool for authors processing regret — time not given, words not said, choices not made. All questions intensity 3. Framing is honest, not guilt-inducing.

questions.prompt: Is there something you didn't do — time you didn't give, words you didn't say — that you want to name?
What do you wish had been different, even if it wasn't anyone's fault?
What do you most regret about the time you had together, and what do you want them to know about that?
follow_up_hints: Use last in this domain. Author must have already opened up.

fear.description: Gated pool for addressing the recipient's fears about the future, or the author's fears about leaving. All questions intensity 3 except one. Framing addresses the fear directly rather than avoiding it.

questions.prompt: Is there something you're afraid this person will struggle with after you're gone?
Is there a fear you imagine they carry — something you'd want to speak to directly in this letter?
What do you want them to know about facing the things they're most afraid of?
follow_up_hints: Lowest-intensity entry in this pool. Safe to surface slightly earlier.

spiritual.description: Gated pool for meaning, legacy, and belief. No faith assumption — questions work for religious, secular, agnostic, and questioning authors. Intensity 2-3.

questions.prompt: What do you find yourself returning to when you think about what matters most?
follow_up_hints: Lowest-intensity entry. Safe opener for this pool.

questions.prompt: What do you want them to know about what has given your life meaning?
What do you hope endures from your life — not achievements, but something more essential?
What do you believe about what happens after we die — not necessarily as doctrine, just as feeling or hope?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Open-ended — secular and religious answers both valid and honored.

questions.prompt: Is there anything you believe about the nature of things — however you'd describe it — that you'd want them to carry?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Deliberately vague framing preserves author's own language.

permission.description: Gated pool for explicit permission-giving — releasing the recipient from grief, guilt, loyalty, or expectation. Intensity 2-3. One of the most important functions a letter like this can serve.

questions.prompt: What do you want them to know about your wishes for their happiness — without condition?
follow_up_hints: Lowest-intensity entry. Safe opener for this pool.

questions.prompt: Is there anything you want to explicitly give them permission to do — be happy, find love again, build a new life?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Most direct permission-giving prompt. Use after hvy-prm-001.

questions.prompt: Is there something they might feel guilty about — something you want to actively release them from?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Covers guilt from the relationship, not just from death.

questions.prompt: What would you want them to give themselves permission for that you're afraid they won't?
follow_up_hints: Gated. Author projects forward — what does this person hold themselves back from?

grief.description: Gated pool for what the author wants the recipient to know about grief — their own grief, and grief as a process. Intensity 2-3. Informed by hospice and palliative care framing: honest, not prescriptive.

questions.prompt: What do you know about getting through loss — from losing others — that you'd want to pass on?
follow_up_hints: Lowest-intensity entry. Safe opener for this pool.

questions.prompt: What do you hope they do in the ordinary days when they miss you most?
What do you want them to know about how you feel about your own death?
follow_up_hints: Gated. One of the most personal and important things this letter can say — if the author is at peace, this communicates it.

questions.prompt: What do you want them to know about grief — not a prescription, but what you hope for them as they move through it?
